parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: On the street above the church, looking down at it.

paras.t: Look down. This small church is Santissima Annunziata dei Catalani. Because of the earthquake of 1908, it now sits 3 meters below the rebuilt street. And it's one of the few buildings in Messina that came through that earthquake at all.
If you go down to it, go slowly and watch your footing.
It's a Norman church. The Normans held Messina from 1060, and the church is usually dated to the 1100s; one listing says the late 1100s into the 1200s, so sources differ slightly.
And the ground under it may be older still. It is said to stand on the ruins of an older temple of Neptune.

parts.name: A mix of worlds
parts.stand: Wherever you get the clearest view of the church walls.

paras.t: What makes it special is the mix. It's Sicilian Norman architecture, with influences from Arab and Byzantine building, and Roman elements too.
Look for the apse. That's the part people single out, because it's unusually well preserved.

Why such a mix? Think of who had ruled here before the Normans came. Messina was Byzantine from 535, then, in the Islamic period, under the Aghlabids and the Fatimids, then Byzantine again from 1038. That's the mix you see in the walls.
The name tells its own story. It used to be called the Annunziata di Castellammare, after a medieval fortress nearby that guarded the entrance to the port and the shipyard.
Its later name, dei Catalani, comes from merchants from Catalonia, who set up in Messina in the 1500s.

One more Catalan echo in Messina: in the days before August 15, two giant statues on horseback, Mata and Grifone, are paraded through the streets. In legend they're the founders of the city, and the giants come from the old Catalan tradition of processional giants.

The city around you was rebuilt from 1912, mostly in the Liberty style. This little church is far older than all of it. It simply stayed where it was, three meters down, while Messina rose up around it.
